title: Is Building Your Own AI the New Path to Attention? — William (Will) Chen of Mike OSS on Legally Disrupted ep. 51
pub: Legally Disrupted ep. 51 (host Zach Abramowitz); recorded 29 May 2026
author: William Chen

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Chen shifts the proposition from specialist vendors defending value through legal workflow layers to well-resourced law firms building those systems internally. His lawyer–engineer team proposal is compatible with contextual collaboration, but he argues that AI software is now sufficiently easy and inexpensive to build that costly external provision may be unnecessary; this is a feasibility claim rather than demonstrated comparative evidence.

qs: Building and releasing a product is a new way to gain attention in legal.
While most critics stop at tweeting or posting cringy safeposts on LinkedIn, Will actually used “vibe coding” tools to build a functioning application layer in just two weeks.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Chen argues that AI-assisted development makes legal-AI application layers easier to reproduce and enables more accessible, locally controlled and firm-specific alternatives to commercial products. Abramowitz separately presents product-building as a new way to attract attention in legal markets.
pts.d: 1. William Chen characterises Harvey and Legora as relatively thin application layers whose substantive functionality does not clearly outperform ChatGPT or Claude. He says he built his open-source alternative in two weeks; this is a claim about reproducing application functionality, not demonstrated enterprise equivalence. 2. Chen argues that AI-assisted coding lets firms build substantial legal software with small teams rather than large engineering organisations. He envisages a technology-literate lawyer or legal engineer paired with software engineers, and suggests that three strong engineers and a legally informed product manager could build and deploy a competing application within a month. 3. Chen nevertheless says coding knowledge remains necessary because AI does not reliably diagnose or repair the errors it creates. 4. Chen claims Mike OSS is already useful for individual lawyers and small teams, but is not currently suitable for AmLaw 200-wide deployment because it lacks enterprise features. He proposes local deployment as a possible workaround and argues that an entirely on-premises application and model can keep documents from reaching third parties. 5. Chen predicts that Mike could become both an intuitive, ready-connected base product for ordinary lawyers and a customisable foundation for well-resourced firms. Firms could add practice-specific extensions and use an inexpensive open-source model to obtain AI at a fraction of third-party vendor costs. 6. Chen argues that legal AI's concentration on luxury-branded products for large firms leaves small and medium firms and the pro bono sector underserved, despite AI's potential to make law more accessible. He also suggests that BigLaw has particularly strong disincentives to use AI properly, without developing that mechanism in detail. 7. Chen reports interest among junior partners and associates in leaving BigLaw and argues that AI creates an unusually favourable opportunity to start lean firms. He positions Mike as a possible enabling tool, not as a demonstrated cause of departures. 8. In his accompanying authored newsletter, Zach Abramowitz argues that building and releasing software is a new route to attention in legal markets. He separately predicts substantial commercial upside for Harvey and Legora and explicitly rejects the proposition that they intend to become AI-first law firms. These are Abramowitz's own positions, not Chen's.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists mainly of Chen's development experience, informal product comparisons, network reports and demonstrations; no systematic performance, cost, security or adoption study is supplied.
pts.d: For claims 1–3, Chen draws on three years practising at Latham & Watkins, roughly ten years of hobby coding, recent use of AI coding tools, demonstrations of Harvey and Legora by acquaintances, and his own comparison of answers to unspecified questions. His impression that little is proprietary partly comes from observing the interfaces; he supplies no backend inspection, test set, scoring method or benchmark. The 85–90% coding-success estimate is experiential, not a measured study. For claim 4, he cites reports from small firms and AI consultants of deployments for teams of approximately ten, individual users' experiences, and online demonstrations of fully local deployments. He explicitly reports no current AmLaw 200 users. His data-sovereignty argument rests on a proposed technical architecture, not a security audit; statements about third-party data handling and contracts are his account, not documented findings of misuse. For claim 5, the cost and usability benefits are prospective, with no comparative cost calculation or user study; the estimate that roughly 80% of lawyers would want a base version has no stated empirical basis. For claim 6, he offers market criticism and references generally to lawyers being castigated by courts over hallucinations, without identifying cases or measuring error rates. For claim 7, the basis is conversations and reports of lawyers considering departure, not employment data or identified firms founded because of Mike. The discussion cites announcements of firm AI investments, especially Kirkland's reported $500 million allocation, as signs of interest in building; these are not evidence of completed deployment or returns. For claim 8, Abramowitz uses Chen's functioning two-week build and public attention as an illustrative case. His expectations for Harvey and Legora are expressed as conviction rather than a financial forecast supported by analysis.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Chen distinguishes current small-scale usefulness from a future enterprise-ready and simpler-to-deploy product; most forecasts have no fixed completion date.
pts.d: The interview was recorded on 29 May 2026 and the accompanying newsletter published on 7 June 2026. Chen places the initial complaints around late 2025 and into 2026, and his product inspection/build initiative around late March 2026. His two-week build is retrospective; the one-month competing-product build is an estimate conditional on recruiting a small, highly capable team. Current coding advice assumes AI still makes errors that require human diagnosis. At interview time, Mike is difficult to deploy and lacks enterprise controls; Chen recommends general-purpose tools as the practical starting point for most lawyers. His local-deployment suggestion requires documents to be copied into the application, creating inconvenience. The strongest closed-loop confidentiality claim requires both the application and an open-source model to run on the firm's own infrastructure; open-source code alone is not the condition he describes. One-click installation, secure hosting, preconnected legal research sources and enterprise features are development intentions rather than completed capabilities. Firm-specific customisation and large cost reductions depend on those improvements, internal resources and a suitable inexpensive model. His favourable outlook for new firms applies to small teams that already have clients and can operate leanly. Abramowitz gives no horizon for the vendors' expected valuation upside.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed changes affect legal-AI vendors, firms choosing whether to build or buy, lawyer-builders, smaller practices, and potentially people excluded from legal help.
pts.d: Harvey and Legora face Chen's proposed competition from reproducible application layers and open-source alternatives, while Abramowitz expects continued commercial upside rather than their displacement or conversion into law firms. Large firms could gain more control over customisation, infrastructure and vendor expenditure, but would need engineering capacity and enterprise safeguards such as organisational controls, audit logging and ethical walls. Technology-literate lawyers, legal engineers, software engineers and product managers are the complementary builders Chen envisages; this is not a prediction that ordinary lawyers can dispense with technical expertise. Individual practitioners and small teams are the reported current users, while less technically confident lawyers are the intended beneficiaries of simpler installation and preconfigured integrations. Junior partners and associates considering departure could use AI to support lean independent firms, although no causal departure outcomes are established. Small and medium firms and pro bono providers are the segments Chen says existing vendor priorities neglect. His broader accessibility argument concerns opening law to more people, but the document does not identify unmet-need populations or demonstrate improved access-to-justice outcomes. Clients' confidential documents and firms' proprietary precedents are the information assets implicated by local hosting. Lawyer-builders and legal technology entrepreneurs may also gain professional visibility through releasing products rather than merely commenting on them.
